Source Title: Active lower limb prosthetics: a systematic review of design issues and solutions
Key Gaps Identified: Identified gaps include the lack of clinical trials comparing powered prostheses to conventional/semi-active devices, heavy reliance on prototypes and small subject numbers necessitating expanded clinical evaluations with commercial devices and diverse gait tasks, unmet engineering challenge to match biological actuation performance while keeping weight and size acceptable, and practical barriers for alternative actuators (e.g., pneumatic PAMs) such as supplying pressure for self-contained systems.
Key Limitations Discussed: Key limitations include fundamental design trade-offs between force/torque output, efficiency, size and weight in actuation units; control strategy limitations such as echo control's inability to support asymmetric or natural interaction; myoelectric control challenges including signal noise, latency and training/proprioception burdens; and the translational gap with many concepts remaining at prototype stage.
Key Recommendations: Recommendations include conducting larger clinical trials using commercial powered prostheses across varied locomotion tasks (incl. slopes, stairs, running); focus actuator development on electromechanical solutions and variable impedance actuators to balance power, efficiency and compliance; and evaluate emerging commercial devices in clinical research to bridge prototype-to-product gap.
Contradictions Or Debates: Debates highlighted include the optimal knee kinematic design (single-axis vs polycentric) with differing recommendations, and trade-offs between actuation principles: electromechanical motors are common despite lower power density, while pneumatic actuators offer better force-to-weight and compliance but have practical supply challenges.

Source Title: A review of user needs to drive the development of lower limb prostheses
Key Gaps Identified: The review identifies several research gaps: the relationship between specific user needs, objective performance measures, and overall satisfaction/quality of life remains unresolved; limited understanding and solutions for social integration, sexual participation, acceptance, appearance, battery life, and clothing/shoe restrictions; lack of commercially available artificial sensory feedback systems despite promising results; poor reporting of prosthesis types in studies, limiting generalizability of findings.
Key Limitations Discussed: Key limitations discussed include: multifaceted, context-dependent and interacting nature of user needs that complicates translation into design; insufficiency of current assessment methods and need for novel, holistic, ecologically valid measures; mismatch between self-reported outcomes and objective measures; laboratory-based gait analyses lacking real-world validity.
Key Recommendations: Recommendations: prioritize user-centered identification of needs to drive prosthesis development; consider additional assessment and development factors recognizing heterogeneous responses to improvements; combine objective measures with subjective impressions and account for inter-subject variability in studies; explore alternative assessment tools like neural correlates and visual sampling to capture cognitive load and real-world function.
Contradictions Or Debates: The paper highlights contradictions between subjective improvements (e.g., increased balance confidence) and objective outcomes (no significant reduction in falls), and more broadly reports a recurring mismatch between self-reports and objective performance measures.

Source Title: Low limb prostheses and complex human prosthetic interaction: A systematic literature review
Main Topic Area: Multiple (design methods, customization, accessibility indirectly via usability and energy, user involvement via HPI)
Key Gaps Identified: The review reports several specific research gaps: lack of a standardised, generalised design structure for new developments; shortcomings in energy management and power/weight trade-offs for battery life and actuator design; absence of generalised machine-learning models for intention recognition and locomotion prediction; need for integrated neural network/deep RL approaches combined with biomechanical models to improve reaction time and autonomous prediction; limited work on multi-degree-of-freedom (2–3 DoF) prostheses balancing performance with weight/size constraints; and immature environment-sensing and perception integration (cameras/IMUs) constrained by processing and weight limits.
Key Limitations Discussed: The paper highlights concrete limitations: many prostheses operate as one-way systems increasing cognitive load on users and lacking bidirectional feedback; EEG/EMG methods suffer from invasiveness (iEMG) or signal noise and unclear methodological reporting (sEMG/EEG electrode placement and data collection); energy and actuator design limit battery life and weight, and control tuning alone cannot resolve fundamental actuator inefficiencies; sensing studies often omit data collection details reducing reproducibility.
Key Recommendations: Recommendations include adopting the paper's proposed generalised design structure as a guideline for future developments; prioritising targeted improvements to individual subsystems (HPI, sensing, electronics, control) sequentially; develop and evaluate energy-efficient, design-specific actuators to reduce weight and extend battery life; pursue integrated ML/deep-RL models combined with biomechanical models for autonomous locomotion prediction and multi-DoF control; and test systems on uneven terrains to improve real-world adaptability.
Contradictions Or Debates: The review notes several tensions and inconsistent findings: EEG and EMG each have advocates—EEG appears more prevalent in studies but is computationally costly while EMG is cheaper but noisier; combining both improves accuracy. Evidence on benefits from increased degrees of freedom is mixed—higher DoF does not always reduce metabolic cost. Locomotion prediction studies report generally high accuracy but have failure modes (e.g., stair descent detection) tied to manual parameter settings, indicating debate over reliability and generalisability of current predictors.

Source Title: Functionality and Comfort Design of Lower-Limb Prosthetics: A Review
Key Gaps Identified: The review identifies several research gaps: need for stronger user-centred design evidence and involvement in design processes; affordability and access to advanced prosthetics, especially cost-effective solutions; unresolved challenges around neural interfaces and sensory feedback integration for natural control; and general gaps in the literature that warrant further study and recommendations.
Key Limitations Discussed: The paper highlights key limitations in current prosthetic design: high cost and training requirements for advanced tech; concerns about long-term performance and durability of components; and persistent issues with socket comfort and skin-related problems.
Key Recommendations: Recommendations include prioritising affordability and accessibility in future designs; adopting and evaluating user-centred design methods to improve satisfaction; and focused R&D on neural interfaces and sensory feedback to enhance control and embodiment.
Contradictions Or Debates: The review notes a tension between rapid technological advances and practical barriers to adoption: while robotics, AI, and sensors promise improved function, adoption is constrained by cost, required training, and customization burdens. No specific contradictory empirical findings are reported; the debate is framed as opportunity versus accessibility constraints.

Source Title: Design Optimization in Lower Limb Prostheses: A Review
Key Gaps Identified: Identified gaps include lack of predictive tools for user performance to guide design optimization, over-reliance on anthropomorphic design that ignores altered post-amputation anatomy, under-exploration of how prosthetic joint behavior affects whole-body gait and user experience, and insufficient integration between experimental parameterization and model-based simulations to improve real-world outcomes.
Key Limitations Discussed: Limitations highlighted are that many designs fail to deliver their hypothesized biomechanical or clinical outcomes consistently, current design approaches are constrained by anthropomorphic assumptions that may not fit altered anatomy, and there is a lack of effective translation from experimental and simulation research into improved real-world prosthesis performance.
Key Recommendations: Recommendations include incorporating predictive tools for user performance into early design optimization, and advancing two research paths—experimental parameterization of designs and model-based simulations—to better predict and improve user outcomes.
Contradictions Or Debates: The paper notes inconsistency between hypothesized design benefits and observed biomechanical outcomes, indicating conflicting or inconclusive evidence about whether current design approaches achieve their intended effects.

Source Title: Active upper limb prostheses: a review on current state and upcoming breakthroughs
Main Topic Area: Multiple (design methods, customization, accessibility, user involvement)
Key Gaps Identified: The review identifies major gaps: high prosthesis abandonment rates linked to insufficiently patient-tailored design; lack of personalization and user-centered development and involvement in design processes; gaps in robust control and sensing—EMG systems' poor robustness and sensitivity to artifacts; insufficient clinical translation of sensory feedback approaches, especially non-invasive feedback; and hurdles for invasive methods (surgical risks, implant compatibility) limiting wider adoption.
Key Limitations Discussed: Key limitations: poor adjustability and limited kinematics and battery/operation time impacting function; low social/personal acceptance driven by poor anthropomorphism, weight, and noise; fundamental instability and noise sensitivity of sEMG/HD-sEMG limiting real-world use; lack of integrated haptic feedback in commercial devices; and stagnation of control paradigms with dated strategies still prevailing.
Key Recommendations: Recommendations: pursue multimodal sensor fusion and multiple input sources plus integrated sensory feedback to enable closed-loop control; prioritize user-centered design, training, and co-adaptive human-machine interfaces to improve acceptance and reduce abandonment; develop modular architectures allowing progressive implant integration and miniaturization for socket embedding.
Contradictions Or Debates: Debates: adequacy of non-invasive signals for robust control—some studies show promise but it's still contested; tension between anthropomorphic design vs. pure functional priorities among users (preferences vary); pace and feasibility of brain-control/neuroprosthetic approaches vs near-term incremental improvements—long-term vision vs short-term deployable solutions.

Source Title: Literature Review on Needs of Upper Limb Prosthesis Users
Key Gaps Identified: The review identifies heterogeneity and methodological gaps across studies, notably inconsistent methods and tools making systematic analysis difficult; lack of common evaluation criteria for user satisfaction which prevents objective comparison across studies; insufficient analysis focused on bilateral amputees and their distinct needs; a translational gap where many control and sensory-feedback solutions remain at research stage without clinical application; and specific limitations of promising approaches (e.g., pattern recognition performs worse in real-world settings and demands long training) that restrict clinical uptake.
Key Limitations Discussed: The paper highlights key limitations: poor, non-intuitive control interfaces that fail to map user intent to prosthetic movement; control methods often need long training and are sensitive to electrode/socket issues leading to signal degradation; invasive neural interfaces face high invasiveness and long-term signal degradation from fibrotic reactions; widespread absence of sensory (tactile/force) feedback and actuator noise reduce functionality and acceptance; and the literature is limited by small, localized studies with heterogeneous methods and selection criteria limiting generalizability.
Key Recommendations: Recommendations include: align design efforts to user priorities to improve satisfaction and reduce abandonment; adopt standardized evaluation metrics (e.g., common Likert-based scales and objective functional tests) to enable cross-study comparison; conduct dedicated, in-depth studies of bilateral amputees to capture their distinct needs; integrate tactile sensorization (contact, sliding, temperature, force) into prostheses to enable force control and sensory feedback; and develop control systems that independently manage finger position and force to reduce visual attention and improve ADL performance.
Contradictions Or Debates: The review notes some tensions rather than direct contradictions: it reports that myoelectric prostheses offer higher dexterity and are more intuitive, yet users of these devices still strongly desire sensory feedback because functionality remains incomplete without afferent signals. Additionally, geographic/cultural differences in prosthesis preference (body-powered in the USA vs cosmetic/myoelectric in Europe) suggest variability driven by cost, occupation and healthcare systems rather than clear superiority of one technology.

Source Title: User experience of transtibial prosthetic liners: A systematic review
Main Topic Area: user involvement / user experience (multiple: customization and design methods secondary)
Key Gaps Identified: Key gaps include insufficient comparative research differentiating user experience across liner types, absence of systematic qualitative studies exploring user perspectives, poor reporting/detail of interventions hindering synthesis, and limited separation of device effects from socket fit or design confounders.
Key Limitations Discussed: Limitations highlighted are pervasive methodological flaws: sampling bias and non-representative samples, use of non-validated outcome measures and inconsistent adaptation of PEQ, poor reporting of interventions and outcomes, and inadequate statistical analyses including uncontrolled multiple comparisons. These reduce internal and external validity and preclude meta-analysis.
Key Recommendations: Recommendations: recruit representative samples reflecting clinical populations; use validated, reliable outcome measures and clearly describe measures and interventions to improve comparability; employ appropriate multivariate statistical methods and report full statistics with effect sizes to enable meta-analysis; and conduct foundational qualitative and observational studies to identify sensitive outcome domains.
Contradictions Or Debates: The paper identifies debates/contradictions: contemporary higher-quality studies suggest elastomer liners may not offer better user experience contrary to earlier positive reports; inconsistencies between objective PEQ scores and user preferences (e.g. Pelite preference despite similar PEQ scores) raise questions about measure sensitivity and interpretation.

Source Title: Effects of lower limb prosthesis on activity, participation, and quality of life: a systematic review
Key Gaps Identified: The paper identifies limited evidence on real-world effectiveness of prostheses and a lack of studies examining how prosthesis systems affect daily life in natural contexts. It highlights inconsistent results and variable study quality, and explicitly calls for high-quality effectiveness studies focused on users' daily living and QoL. The review also notes that key factors influencing effectiveness remain unexplored and require further research.
Key Limitations Discussed: The review highlights methodological limitations across included studies: small sample sizes, short follow-up durations, heterogeneity of interventions and outcome measures, and variable internal/external validity scores. It also notes reliance on laboratory/efficacy studies in the field and the challenge of conducting high-level evidence studies that still capture daily-life effectiveness.
Key Recommendations: The authors recommend conducting high-quality effectiveness studies in real-world contexts focusing on activity, participation, and QoL to inform clinical guidelines. They call for standardised, clinically relevant outcome measures and larger, longer follow-up studies to determine key factors affecting prosthetic effectiveness.
Contradictions Or Debates: The paper documents contradictory findings across studies, especially regarding the benefits of microprocessor-controlled knees (MP-knee) versus non-microprocessor knees (NMP-knee): some studies report QoL and use improvements and reduced falls, others report no difference in activity or satisfaction. This inconsistency indicates active debate and uncertainty about which prosthetic interventions reliably improve daily-life outcomes.

Key Recommendations: Recommendations include basing prosthetic prescriptions on matching prosthetic functional benefits to user functional needs, and integrating research evidence with clinical expert opinion and consumer preferences to develop guideline procedures for prosthetic prescription.
Contradictions Or Debates: The paper indicates a lack of consensus on prescription criteria, implying debate or inconsistent findings across the literature regarding which components best serve specific user needs.

Key Limitations Discussed: Technical and practical limitations include sensor cost, limited battery life and limited availability preventing routine clinical use. Research limitations include small sample sizes and short monitoring durations, reducing power and generalisability. Outcome measures are insensitive (step-counts only) and algorithms/tools are not user-friendly for clinicians. Additional systemic barriers include lack of training, capacity, cultural concerns, and infrastructure (connectivity, electricity) especially in low-resource settings.
Key Recommendations: Combine activity monitoring with clinical scores and user feedback for richer evaluation of prosthesis function <citations>0</citations]. Develop and validate algorithms to classify activity types from prosthesis-mounted sensors (including below-knee locations) <citations>1</citations]. Source Title: Adjustable prosthetic sockets: a systematic review of industrial and research design characteristics and their justifications
Main Topic Area: design methods, customization, accessibility, and user involvement (multiple)
Key Gaps Identified: The review identifies several explicit research gaps: the relationship between socket design and comfort/function is rarely investigated; a disconnect between industry and academic focus, with different design emphases and limited published evaluation of commercial products; lack of justification and standardized reporting for adjustment locations and ranges; absence of research defining objective metrics for a 'well-fitting' socket; many commercial designs lack supporting clinical studies (68.75% unsupported); and limited research on suitability and application in low-resource settings.
Key Limitations Discussed: The paper highlights key limitations in the evidence base: small study sizes and predominance of case or cohort studies with few randomized or long-term trials, and only 17.6% evaluated commercial devices; safety features are often absent or unreported, risking tissue damage or poor coupling; underreporting of adverse events (only five studies reported them) and short-term follow-up limit safety and durability assessment; and the review itself is limited by not physically inspecting commercial sockets, requiring assumptions from patents and descriptions.
Key Recommendations: Recommendations include: prioritise research on adjustable sockets in low-resource settings; improve collaboration and knowledge exchange between academia and industry to evaluate commercial devices and align research to practice; conduct rigorous studies to define objective metrics for a well-fitting socket and to investigate relationships between design, mechanical coupling, comfort, and tissue health; assess comfort systematically across adjustment levels and locations; and apply scientific evaluation to commercial designs to identify which patient subgroups benefit most.
Contradictions Or Debates: The paper identifies debates and contradictions: industry and research pursue different design approaches with limited cross-evaluation, leading to uncertainty about which designs are most effective; reported comfort improvements lack mechanistic explanations and consistent measurement, producing conflicting interpretations of benefit; and some study demonstrations (e.g., motor-driven panel-induced fluid recovery) show promising tissue effects but rely on actuation methods not feasible in typical clinical devices, raising questions about real-world applicability.

Source Title: Design, Kinematics and Gait Analysis, of Prosthetic Knee Joints: A Systematic Review
Key Gaps Identified: The review identifies several research gaps: a need for powered/active prosthetic knee designs that meet amputees' requirements; insufficient work on uphill/ramp locomotion and inclined-surface kinematics; lack of intent-recognition (volitional) control for stairs and other modes; underdeveloped active EMG-based transfemoral prostheses for robust real-time control; and a shortage of real-time testing on amputees (many studies use models, healthy subjects, or virtual environments).
Key Limitations Discussed: The paper highlights limitations including lack of comfort and reliability in commercial prostheses; passive hydraulic/pneumatic designs with fixed impedance that cannot adapt to varied locomotion; many active designs are complex and remain in labs without real-time amputee testing; material constraints (e.g., CFRP poor conductivity for active systems).
Key Recommendations: Recommendations include: develop EMG-based electromechanical transfemoral prostheses for intent recognition and volitional control; implement real-time testing on amputees (not only simulations or healthy subjects); consider energy/torque/impedance control designs and regeneration methods to power active prostheses; and provide adequate user training prior to deployment.
Contradictions Or Debates: The paper notes mixed findings and trade-offs: while microprocessor-controlled knees generally outperform non-microprocessor ones, hybrid designs may sacrifice stability; studies vary in which biomechanical parameters are met, indicating inconsistent evidence across prototypes. It emphasizes consensus that closed-loop active control is necessary for stable volitional ambulation.

Contradictions Or Debates: The paper notes debates around optimal control modalities: while surface EMG predominates, alternative methods like FMG claim advantages (cheaper, more accurate, more stable). There's also tension between adding actuators and gestures (improving functionality) versus the resulting weight and balance trade-offs, and differing emphases on customization versus mass-market commercial designs reflected across patents, scientific articles, and commercial products.

Contradictions Or Debates: The paper reports debated/incongruent findings: self-reported satisfaction often conflicts with objective problems (e.g., swelling) suggesting resignation or psychological adaptation, literature shows discrepancies between short-term reported benefit of advanced components and longer-term real-world activity outcomes.

Source Title: Haptic Feedback Systems for Lower-Limb Prosthetic Applications: A Review of System Design, User Experience, and Clinical Insights

Contradictions Or Debates: The paper notes debates around presentation timing for multichannel vibrotactile patterns: simultaneous presentation can be faster but risks confusion, whereas sequential presentation yields higher accuracy in pattern recognition. Additionally, modality trade-offs (vibrotactile vs electrotactile vs mechanotactile) present conflicting advantages in resolution, comfort, and practicality discussed across studies.

Key Limitations Discussed: Limitations highlighted include technical constraints in actuator and kinematic design and immature control algorithms for replicating biological function across speeds and transitions; reliance on passive solutions with limited energy storage/return motivating compliant actuation but indicating current limitations in energy-efficient designs; and limited consideration of psychological human factors (acceptance and body schema integration) in current prosthetic development that constrain adoption and design relevance.
Key Recommendations: Recommend pursuing compliant actuator and kinematic designs for energy storage/transfer; developing bio-inspired controllers that handle different gait situations, speeds, and transitions; integrating comprehensive biomechanical analyses (with and without prostheses) to derive design requirements and constraints; and systematically incorporating human factors research—using psychological survey methods—into the design process to improve acceptance and embodiment.
Contradictions Or Debates: The paper notes a tension between technological advancement towards powered/robotic prostheses and the human factors challenges of acceptance and embodiment: while biomechanical evidence suggests active prostheses improve gait, their integration into users' body schema and acceptance remains challenging. This reflects a debate on prioritizing technical performance versus user-centred psychosocial outcomes.

Source Title: Towards Including End-Users in the Design of Prosthetic Hands: Ethical Analysis of a Survey of Australians with Upper-Limb Difference

Key Recommendations: Recommend incorporating end-user engagement and co-design into prosthetic design processes, developing methods for meaningful user involvement; adopt a relational autonomy framework to orient design towards supporting users' valued activities and choices rather than only restoring 'normal' form; prioritise affordability and customisable aesthetics to reflect diverse preferences and improve accessibility; use richer qualitative methods (interviews, focus groups, co-design) to capture contextual and identity-related factors.
Contradictions Or Debates: Identifies debates over framing non-use: as a user problem (lack of adaptation), as a design problem (device limitations), or as non-problematic (social model). Notes empirical tension: technological advancement/ sophistication does not reliably increase uptake, contradicting assumptions that better tech equals greater use.

Key Limitations Discussed: Highlights practical and methodological limitations: high cost, limited sensor battery-life and poor availability limiting clinical adoption; small sample sizes and high inter-individual variability reducing power to detect component differences; analysis tools and algorithms are not user-friendly, requiring technical skill; and cultural, contextual and logistical barriers (privacy, follow-up, infrastructure) affecting monitoring in low-resource settings.
Key Recommendations: Recommend developing a coordinated framework for out-of-clinic monitoring sensitive to low-resource contexts; use sensors that provide raw data for bespoke analyses and reproducibility; adopt user-centred design and consider acceptability/privacy in monitoring tools; create shared datasets with metadata standards to enable cross-study comparisons and early-warning use cases.
Contradictions Or Debates: Notes apparent contradictions: many component-comparison studies report no significant differences, but the review argues this may be due to methodological constraints rather than true equivalence. Also highlights discrepancy between clinic-based functional measures (e.g., K-level) and real-world activity, suggesting conflicting interpretations between lab assessments and community monitoring.

Contradictions Or Debates: The paper notes unclear and inconsistent evidence on AT coverage across studies, a disconnect between prevalence estimates and explanatory evidence due to methodological heterogeneity, and conflicting or variable prevalence findings across impairment types and age groups (e.g., higher met-need rates for sensory impairments but wide variation overall) attributed to differing data collection strategies.

Key Limitations Discussed: The paper highlights limitations including poor AT design, production and execution contributing to abandonment; systemic barriers such as communication, ethical concerns, time and cost constraints that hinder design engagement with AT practice; high abandonment rates (~30% in first year) emphasizing the scale of the problem; and siloed practices between design and healthcare leading to unsustainable interventions.

Contradictions Or Debates: The paper notes tensions between optimism for design methods' benefits and practical challenges in integrating designers into healthcare research (e.g., some studies used design methods without designers). Source Title: Impediments to Assistive Technology Accessibility for Students With Disabilities in Higher Education Institutions: A Systematic Review

Key Recommendations: Recommend future research (bibliometric/extended reviews) to map trends and impacts and to explore frameworks for awareness and capacity-building; adopt Universal Design for Learning principles in AT design; HEIs should implement clear policies, guidelines and institutional capacity building for AT provision and maintenance; and invest in instructor training and user involvement in AT design and follow-up to reduce abandonment.
Contradictions Or Debates: The paper does not report major contradictions but highlights tensions: global commitments (SDGs/WHO) versus persistent real-world gaps in HEIs, especially in low-income settings; and differing experiences across countries with high-income versus low/middle-income contexts showing inconsistent service quality and access. It also notes debated causes of abandonment (design mismatch vs. lack of follow-up) reflected in literature.

It also highlights limited empirical evidence on whether standards (like ISO 9241-210) drive innovation or improved outcomes, indicating uncertainty in the field.

Source Title: Estimating need and coverage for five priority assistive products: a systematic review of global population-based research
Main Topic Area: accessibility (assistive product need and coverage) and data/measurement methods (design methods & reporting); multiple
Key Gaps Identified: The review identifies major gaps including lack of standardised AP data collection and reporting leading to incomparable indicators, sparse evidence from LMICs where needs are greatest, inconsistent definitions of AP access terms causing over/underestimation of need, limited research on effectiveness and follow-up of AT interventions, and uneven topic coverage with vision overrepresented while mobility, hearing and cognition are underrepresented.
Key Limitations Discussed: The paper highlights limitations including heterogeneous assessment methods mixing clinical and self-report approaches limiting comparability, reliance on secondary analyses and small primary samples for mobility studies reducing robustness, inability to perform meta-analysis due to reporting variation, and possible missed studies because search terms used 'functional difficulty' rather than specific conditions.
Key Recommendations: Key recommendations are to establish a global minimum AP dataset with standardised measures, AP lists, indicators and measurement approaches; collect holistic data including personal and environmental factors and test methods in diverse contexts especially LMICs; integrate AP indicator modules into established population surveys for better secondary analyses; and distinguish AP use from met need to detect undermet need among users.
Contradictions Or Debates: The paper identifies debates about appropriate assessment methods: equating functional difficulty prevalence with AP need vs. nuanced clinical and personal-factor assessments can lead to conflicting estimates. Economic evaluations are absent: "Economic and cost-benefit analyses of available devices are not discussed by the researchers, which is an essential factor in the usage of rehabilitation devices." Safety outcomes for caregivers and users are unstudied: "Caregiver injury and the individual user's injury in the absence of a caregiver have not been studied." The paper also highlights broad unresolved areas and need for research and affordability/technology maturation: "Most of the reviewed research on assistive devices is marked by the rapid development of the field, yet, at the same time, there are gaps and scope for further research." and "Hardware and software development are required to bring affordable assistive devices to a wider population that needs them."
Key Limitations Discussed: The paper highlights device-level limitations including potential bias from caregiver-reported data: "A likely drawback of the proposed game is that the caregivers' involvement may potentially provide biased and less valid answers (4)." It notes some wearable or sensing systems are unsuitable for lower-functioning users: "The limitation of the wearable device is that it used a bidirectional conversational module and wearable eye tracker which is not suitable for less-functioning individuals with autism." Mechanical and actuator issues (bulky, heavy, high energy use) are raised: "However, the actuator devices were bulky, stiff, consumed more energy, and heavy." Fit and comfort concerns are repeatedly mentioned: "Comfort and fit on wearing the device had to be taken care of." Sensing/measurement limitations (image blurring) and usability/cost trade-offs are discussed: "However, deformation may lead to modifications in muscle morphology, resulting in a blurry image and reducing the accuracy of segmentation." and "the inconvenience of wearing a headset and the high cost of the device are trade-offs of the device."
Key Recommendations: Recommendations include pursuing future research on individual care, learning, and computer accessibility using assistive devices: "Future research pathways relating to individual care using assistive devices for learning and computer accessibility are analyzed." The authors call for hardware and software development to make affordable devices widely available: "Hardware and software development are required to bring affordable assistive devices to a wider population that needs them." They also suggest leveraging assistive-device research to inform other disease areas: "This review emphasizes how most of the research on assistive devices can help advance research on other diseases." and more broadly state "There is a need for further research and development in the field of assistive technology which is likely to expand tremendously in the future."
Contradictions Or Debates: The paper notes inconsistencies and incomplete evidence in evaluated studies: it states behavioral studies in autism lacked data to determine social significance and that user tests often lacked acceptance/validation information: "The study analyzed the behavioral studies that were done in past but found no data to ascertain whether the observed behaviors were socially significant." and "The studies presented more user test results but their acceptance and validations were not included." It also highlights trade-offs in performance claims (e.g. high accuracy in constrained settings but tradeoffs in speed and generalisability): "With less available training data, speakerbased automatic speech recognizers with mini vocabularies were built... The trade-offs were in message production speed and data outcomes range."

Source Title: A systematic literature review on user centered design and participatory design with older people
Key Gaps Identified: The paper identifies gaps in guidance and methods for involving older adults in UCD/PD processes, noting that UCD/PD "provide little guidance on how to involve older people in the development process". It highlights that "Traditional design methods may not be sufficient" for older users and that there is a scarcity of detailed reporting on how participatory activities are conducted with older people. The review also points to insufficient research and guidance on requirements elicitation and prototyping tailored to older adults, and a lack of methods accommodating geographically dispersed participants or contexts where group activities are impracticable.
Key Limitations Discussed: The paper discusses practical limitations in current practice: many older adults lack ICT skills limiting meaningful participation; studies often involve seniors only at late stages or only conduct usability tests post-development; logistical barriers such as mobility constrain attendance at workshops/interviews; and overall, traditional UCD/PD methods require adaptation to be effective with older adults.
Key Recommendations: The authors recommend involving older adults throughout all development stages, conducting longitudinal studies spanning from early design to deployment, developing new engagement strategies and clearer methods for requirements elicitation, and applying Action Research to adapt prototyping and processes to older adults' needs. They also emphasize continued involvement across the whole design process.
Contradictions Or Debates: The paper notes tensions in practice: while PD ideally involves older users throughout, many studies are expert-centered or only include seniors late in development, creating a debate about the extent and timing of involvement. It also raises a caution that older participants' limited ICT experience can both limit contributions and bias outcomes by focusing on familiar solutions.

Source Title: Assessing the implementation of user-centred design standards on assistive technology for persons with visual impairments: A systematic review
Main Topic Area: user involvement (User-Centred Design) and design methods (application of ISO 9241-210)
Key Gaps Identified: The review identifies several research gaps: insufficient evidence that UCD implementation leads to innovation, improved access, wellbeing or satisfaction; inconsistent and shallow characterization of user needs and contexts, especially in early design and prototyping phases; poor reporting and lack of multidisciplinary design teams; and limited evaluation in real-world scenarios (external validity).
Key Limitations Discussed: The paper highlights limitations in the existing literature: generally low methodological quality across studies with many failing MMAT criteria; poor sampling practices and small, non-representative samples in quantitative studies; weak, anecdotal reporting of user feedback and lack of rigorous qualitative reporting; and failure to characterize social, physical and infrastructural contexts affecting device use.
Key Recommendations: Recommendations: improve and standardize UCD implementation in AT projects and build stronger evidence linking UCD to outcomes; provide capacity building and planning for UCD within development teams and promote cross-disciplinary collaboration between engineering, social, clinical sciences and disability stakeholders; ensure meaningful user involvement throughout all design stages; adopt transdisciplinary teams to address methodological flaws and contextual needs.
Contradictions Or Debates: The review notes conceptual debate: whether to use a strictly 'user-centred' approach (focus on product–user interaction) versus a 'person-centred' approach (broader context, meaning and agency) and finds most studies adopt the narrower user-centred trend. There is also discussion about the degree of multidisciplinary involvement—standards do not mandate breadth but the authors argue transdisciplinarity is needed to address complex contextual needs.

Contradictions Or Debates: The paper notes a tension/contradiction: although the literature champions user involvement, empirical evidence does not consistently show that involvement leads to greater adoption — i.e., user involvement is necessary but not sufficient.

Source Title: Assessing the implementation of user-centred design standards on assistive technology for persons with visual impairments: a systematic review
Main Topic Area: user involvement (User-Centred Design), design methods, accessibility, customization (multiple)
Key Gaps Identified: The review identifies several research gaps: inconsistent and shallow understanding of user needs, poor characterization and reporting of UCD application especially in early design and prototyping; insufficient evidence to assess UCD's impact on innovation, access, wellbeing, or satisfaction; emphasis on system requirements over context-of-use and user preferences, with limited real-world evaluation; poor citation and explicit use of ISO 9241-210 in most studies indicating lack of standardized application; and geographic gaps with almost all studies from high-income countries and none from low-income settings.
Key Limitations Discussed: Major limitations across reviewed studies include generally low methodological quality with only four meeting all MMAT criteria; poor quantitative sampling practices—non-probability samples, unspecified selection criteria, and small sizes; superficial and anecdotal user feedback rather than systematic qualitative data collection; limited testing in real-world contexts; and lack of multidisciplinary teams limiting breadth of perspectives.

Contradictions Or Debates: The review highlights some debates and contradictions: many studies claim to use UCD but rarely reference formal standards (ISO 9241-210), indicating a discrepancy between claimed and documented practice; there is a conceptual debate between 'user-centred' versus 'person-centred' approaches, with most studies following the narrower user-centred trend while fewer adopt a person-centred perspective that accounts for broader context and meaning; and justifications for limited real-world testing vary (preliminary research vs non-commercial aims), revealing inconsistent rationales that complicate assessing generalizability.

Source Title: Design Approaches for Creating Person-Centered, Context Sensitive, and Sustainable Assistive Technology with the Global South
Study Type: Book chapter / literature review / critical discussion paper
Main Topic Area: multiple (design methods; customization; accessibility; user involvement)
Key Gaps Identified: The chapter identifies large access gaps to assistive technologies in LMICs, noting only 5-15% coverage; major design flaws that prevent technologies (especially ETAs) from reaching most visually impaired users; knowledge gaps on ICT penetration and affordability (smartphones/internet) in LMICs that undermine tech-based solutions; and a lack of evidence about which technologies work for which people in which contexts, indicating unmet needs for context-specific effectiveness research.
Key Limitations Discussed: The chapter highlights multiple limitations: designs biased toward high-income contexts; high cost placing ETAs out of reach for most LMIC users; usability barriers including complexity and training requirements; ergonomic issues such as weight and discomfort; poor aesthetics leading to rejection by users; and broader socioeconomic/contextual mismatches (safety, infrastructure, taxation) that invalidate transferred technologies.
Key Recommendations: Recommendations include adopting person-centered, context-sensitive design approaches; meaningful, diverse user involvement and co-design from early phases; real-world testing in daily routines; inclusion of sustainable business/value-chain models to ensure scale and availability; using the capabilities approach as a theoretical framework to guide design priorities beyond bodily deficit; and North–South cooperation with careful re-contextualization rather than direct technology transfer.
Contradictions Or Debates: The chapter notes tensions rather than strict contradictions: it acknowledges international policy progress (CRPD, Dubai Declaration) while arguing that practical outcomes lag; it debates transferability—some solutions may be mutually beneficial across North/South, others not, stressing re-contextualization rather than direct transfer; and it highlights a critical debate about dominant disability scholarship being Northern-centric and producing technologies that reinforce exclusion in the Global South.

Key Limitations Discussed: Highlights practical limitations of current STS devices (bulkiness, poor accessibility, stigma/unacceptability of exoskeletons) and research limitations including small, self-selected sample and imprecise self-report measures.
Key Recommendations: Recommend early and sustained user-centered/co-design methods, use of prototyping (look-and-feel, works-like, Wizard of Oz) to elicit latent needs, and measuring aesthetic/subjective metrics (look-and-feel) alongside functional metrics to improve adoption.
Contradictions Or Debates: Documents a contradiction between objective mobility measures/expert ratings and older adults' self-perception of need: participants often underreport difficulty despite clinical indicators of fall risk, creating a tension between clinical assessment and user acceptance of assistive devices.

Source Title: Participatory and Inclusive Design Models from the Perspective of Universal Design for Children with Autism: A Systematic Review
Main Topic Area: user involvement; design methods; customization (adaptive/universal design); accessibility (multiple)
Key Gaps Identified: The review identifies multiple research gaps: limited quantity of high-quality studies meeting inclusion criteria, necessitating an expanded timeframe; widespread lack of adaptive methods in research (58.82% without adaptive methods); poor reporting or absence of methods to identify children's interests, skills, and needs (majority do not clarify profiling); frequent absence of direct child participation in design stages (some studies used proxies only); scarcity of adaptive tools tailored to autism diversity (only 14 tools reported); and limited conceptual clarity/consistency in terminology and keyword grouping across studies affecting synthesis.
Key Limitations Discussed: The paper highlights several limitations in current practice: prevalent omission of adaptive methods in studies (limiting applicability to diverse autism profiles); poor user profiling and scarce reporting of participant characteristics (only six studies detailed user profiles); challenges and ethical/practical difficulties in directly involving children with autism leading to reliance on proxies; concentration of work on communication (23/34) potentially leaving social and learning needs less addressed; and a general risk that rapidly evolving computational tools are not designed with accessibility/universal design in mind.
Key Recommendations: Recommendations include: develop adaptive hardware and software following inclusive and universal design principles; ensure active, sustained participation of children with autism in PD across all R&D stages rather than relying on proxies; use blended/mixed methods (merging techniques) and involve health professionals, educators, and parents to capture diverse insights and adapt designs to individual profiles; improve user profiling and reporting to better tailor interventions and evaluations.
Contradictions Or Debates: The paper notes tensions rather than explicit empirical contradictions: some studies rely on designer-led approaches without stakeholder involvement while PD proponents argue for transformative benefits of participatory approaches. There is debate over feasibility of direct participation (practical/ethical barriers) versus the necessity of direct involvement to achieve inclusive outcomes; this creates a split in methods (proxy-based vs. direct PD) and uneven adoption of adaptive methods.

Contradictions Or Debates: The paper highlights debates rather than direct contradictions: variability exists between studies that claim to use formal HCD frameworks and those that do not apply them consistently, creating tensions in assessing efficacy and transferability. There is an ongoing debate about balancing rapid technological innovation (e.g., AR, robotics, AI) with meaningful stakeholder inclusion, where cutting-edge developments are sometimes pursued without adequate user involvement, raising concerns about accessibility and relevance.

Source Title: Perceived barriers and opportunities to the use of 3D printing in a healthcare system with low adoption: A semi-structured interview study
Main Topic Area: additive manufacturing in healthcare — design methods/customization/accessibility/user involvement (multiple)
Key Gaps Identified: Identifies lack of large-scale clinical effectiveness and safety studies for 3D printing in healthcare, a paucity of technology assessment research on 3D printing and its impacts on adoption, and limited generalisability from single-region studies indicating need for broader, international research.
Key Limitations Discussed: Highlights low awareness among HCPs and limited access to printers and expertise, shortages of specialist staffing and infrastructure in many facilities, systemic pressures and competing priorities that deprioritise innovation, and potential role disruption, regulatory and quality concerns from shifting production in-house.
Key Recommendations: Recommend raising awareness and implementing education/interventions for HCPs about 3D printing benefits and uses; consider hub-and-spoke models with point-of-care facilities acting as regional hubs to share expertise and resources; and conduct broader international and technology-assessment research to establish evidence of effectiveness and safety.
Contradictions Or Debates: Documents debates among HCPs about education (whether 3D printing belongs in undergraduate curricula), tensions between innovation and resource-constrained priorities—innovation seen as a 'luxury' vs potential adjunct to care, and concerns about role displacement and disruption of existing supply relationships and regulatory/legal implications.

Source Title: A Case Study: Can 3D printers be used to address the prosthetic needs of amputees in the Dominican Republic?
Study Type: Thesis / case study with literature review (not a formal systematic review)
Main Topic Area: multiple (additive manufacturing/3D printing, customization, accessibility, user involvement)
Key Gaps Identified: Identifies limited formal research and lack of standardized procedures for 3D-printed lower-limb prosthetics, gaps in published evidence representing field practice, and limited data on long-term device lifespan and repairs.
Key Limitations Discussed: Highlights systemic limitations: fragmented institutional responsibilities and accountability, resulting monetary and transport barriers to access, and limited technical education/information among practitioners and decision-makers.
Key Recommendations: Recommends adopting 3D printing (or hybrid) for cost reduction and decentralization, streamlining government infrastructure or establishing a public-private alliance (PPA) with ADR as lead, partnering with experienced NGOs for training/transition, and promoting technical education and assessment protocols.
Contradictions Or Debates: Notes tension between promising pilot/NGO-driven results and limited formal research/standards, especially for lower-limb devices; i.e., enthusiasm from case studies contrasts with lack of standardized evidence and long-term evaluation.

Source Title: The Current State of 3D-Printed Prostheses Clinical Outcomes: A Systematic Review
Main Topic Area: Customization; design methods; accessibility; user involvement (multiple)
Key Gaps Identified: Identified gaps include small sample sizes and limited high-quality evidence, lack of randomized controlled trials and rigorous study designs, heterogeneous and non-standardized outcome measures and assessment tools hindering comparability, and absence of studies on certain prosthetic types (e.g., above-knee devices).
Key Limitations Discussed: Key limitations highlighted are frequent device durability and component breakage issues, heterogeneity and lack of standardized assessment tools for patient-reported outcomes, technical/process limitations in digital workflows such as limited tactile feedback, post-processing needs, and printer variability, and generally low methodological quality across studies with most rated fair or poor.
Key Recommendations: Recommendations include conducting well-designed, larger clinical trials with standardized outcome measures and long-term follow-up, developing standardized evaluation protocols and studying long-term durability and broader prosthetic applications, and addressing regulatory, material, and technical barriers to facilitate clinical adoption.
Contradictions Or Debates: The paper notes conflicting findings: in some studies able-bodied users performed better with 3D-printed hands while users with amputations performed better with traditional hooks, indicating variability in device effectiveness across user populations. It also highlights a debate over durability versus accessibility—3D-printed devices improve access and customization but face durability and evidence-quality concerns.

Source Title: 3D-printed prostheses in developing countries: A systematic review
Key Gaps Identified: The review identifies a lack of clear evidence on sustainability and scalability of 3D-printed prostheses in lower-income and lower-middle-income countries, noting uncertainty about whether 3D-printing can provide a sustainable solution. It also highlights insufficient and heterogeneous published data on outcomes (costs, weight, technology, user satisfaction, failure rates), indicating a need for more rigorous, standardized research and reporting to build broader knowledge for LLMIC contexts.
Key Limitations Discussed: The paper highlights limitations including material scarcity and high cost barriers in LLMICs that impede prosthesis availability. It also notes that while 3D-printing can lower costs and provide patient-specific components, practical limitations remain in manufacturing and postprocessing capacity and in the evidence base because included studies were limited to interventions in LLMICs and varied in measures reported.
Key Recommendations: Recommend more rigorous, standardized scientific research and publication on 3D-printed prostheses in LLMICs, including consistent reporting on cost, weight, printing technologies, user satisfaction, and failure rates to assess effectiveness and scalability.
Contradictions Or Debates: Not mentioned in source.

Source Title: A scoping review of digital fabrication techniques applied...
Main Topic Area: design methods, customization, accessibility, user involvement (multiple)
Key Gaps Identified: Key gaps identified include lack of long-term, large-scale studies, paucity of formal peer-reviewed studies for mature/commercial systems despite market use, minimal research on training and maintenance requirements for personnel using digital fabrication equipment, scarce research specifically on modification/rectification practices post-fabrication, and unclear data on the numbers, outcomes, and geographic distribution of clinical use of digital technologies.
Key Limitations Discussed: Limitations highlighted: predominance of low TRL proof-of-concept studies with limited real-world/long-term testing; frequent omission of critical postprocessing and adjustments in methods reporting; sparse qualitative outcome data and ON-patient long-term evaluations; concerns about material properties, strength and durability of AM-produced devices; and incomplete reporting of materials used.
Key Recommendations: Recommendations: conduct larger, long-term, and higher-TRL clinical studies and translate in-house/industry R&D into peer-reviewed trials; increase collaboration between academia, industry and clinical teams across the pathway to market; improve visibility and reporting of clinical use, outcomes and geographic spread of digital fabrication systems.
Contradictions Or Debates: Contradictions/debates: tension between authors advocating low-cost FDM scaling and lack of scaled implementation; mixed comparative outcomes between printed and conventional devices across different sites (e.g., Tanzania vs other sites) indicating inconsistent effectiveness findings; discrepancy between commercial market readiness claims and paucity of peer-reviewed longitudinal evidence.

Source Title: 3D Printing in the Creation of Orthopedic Prostheses and Orthoses
Key Gaps Identified: The review identifies major research gaps including lack of standardization in 3D printing protocols, insufficient long-term clinical outcome data to validate durability and safety, and technical barriers to wider clinical adoption. It also calls for the creation of systematized data, protocols and standards of conduct, and further research to better understand and implement 3D printing in clinical practice.
Key Limitations Discussed: The paper highlights limitations including lack of standardized study protocols and clinical procedures, limited long-term safety and performance data, and technical constraints of materials (e.g., insufficient mechanical strength of some bioinks/bioceramics) that prevent standalone use in load-bearing applications.
Key Recommendations: Recommendations include developing standardized protocols and reporting, conducting long-term clinical validation studies, and focused research to improve material mechanical properties and biocompatibility to enable load-bearing applications and broader clinical adoption.
Contradictions Or Debates: The review notes ambiguous and sometimes conflicting results: while many studies report benefits of 3D printing (customization, comfort, reduced costs), some evidence suggests conventional materials remain superior in certain load-bearing or durability contexts, indicating debate over where 3D-printed solutions are preferable.

Source Title: 3D-printed prostheses in developing countries: A systematic review
Key Gaps Identified: The paper identifies a lack of clear evidence that 3D-printing can sustainably address low prosthesis availability in lower-income countries, and highlights insufficient and non-homogeneous published data on 3D-printed prostheses for LLMICs, indicating a need for more scientific research and consistent reporting.
Key Limitations Discussed: The review notes limitations in the current evidence base: studies are heterogeneous and limited in scope, reporting primarily descriptive outcomes such as cost, weight, satisfaction and failure rate rather than long-term effectiveness or sustainability. While 3D-printed prostheses show promise due to low material costs, aesthetics and personalization, the review implies these advantages are not yet proven at scale or over time.
Key Recommendations: The authors recommend more (scientific) published research with standardized, homogeneous data on 3D-printed prostheses in LLMICs to assess sustainability and broader applicability, and continued use of systematic search approaches across major databases to capture evidence.
Contradictions Or Debates: Not mentioned in source.

Source Title: 3D-printed orthoses and prostheses for people with physical disability in rehabilitation centers: a scoping review
Main Topic Area: Customization; design methods; accessibility; user involvement (multiple)
Key Gaps Identified: Identifies gaps in clinical evidence and validation: lack of long-term follow-up data on efficacy, safety, durability, comfort, weight, and dimensions of 3D-printed devices; inadequate sample sizes/participant representation and need for broader amputee validation of CAD/3DP methods.
Key Limitations Discussed: Highlights material and performance limitations: problems with force transmission, rigidity, resistance, durability, weight (heavier/bulkier designs to match resistance), and task performance (grip slipping).
Key Recommendations: Recommends: larger clinical studies with long-term follow-up assessing efficacy, safety, durability, comfort, weight, dimensions, and ease of use; broaden participant validation (more amputees) for CAD/3DP methods; collaboration between clinical and research communities to develop useful digital tools.
Contradictions Or Debates: Identifies a tension: while many studies report successful, time-efficient manufacture and positive functional outcomes, persistent material and performance limitations (rigidity, force, resistance) create conflicting impressions about readiness for clinical adoption.

Source Title: 3D Printing in Prosthetics, Orthotics and Assistive Technology: Myth and Reality
Key Gaps Identified: The paper identifies gaps in evidence and data supporting objective design decisions in prosthetics/orthotics, stressing that 3D printing is a tool not a solution and that interdisciplinary collaboration is lacking and needed to translate AM developments into clinical value.
Key Limitations Discussed: The paper highlights limitations including concerns over mechanical robustness of 3D-printed components and fit-related harms, and emphasizes that technology alone (printers) cannot substitute for clinical expertise.
Key Recommendations: Recommendations focus on interdisciplinary collaboration and inclusion of prosthetists/orthotists throughout research and development, and on clinicians engaging with digital production chains to ensure clinical relevance and safe adoption.
Contradictions Or Debates: The paper notes a debate between public/enthusiast expectations that 3D printing would disrupt prosthetics and clinician skepticism about robustness and fit, but does not present conflicting empirical findings; rather it frames a tension between optimism and clinical caution.

Source Title: Overcoming Challenges and Innovations in Orthopedic Prosthesis Design: An Interdisciplinary Perspective
Key Gaps Identified: The paper highlights gaps in access and equity for prosthetic devices in developing countries, challenges in technology/materials and R&D for upper-limb prostheses affecting user suitability, and limited evidence on biomechanical and clinical outcomes for patient-specific/customized implants.
Key Limitations Discussed: The paper discusses limitations including potential toxicity and emissions from additive manufacturing materials used in prosthetics, insufficient and inconsistent methods for measuring interface stresses within prosthetic sockets, and fragmented practice due to lack of multidisciplinary, user-centred approaches in design and deployment.
Key Recommendations: Recommendations emphasise adopting multidisciplinary, user-centred design practices to improve access and suitability of prosthetics, and further research into patient-specific/customized implants to establish biomechanical and clinical benefits.
Contradictions Or Debates: The paper references areas with differing viewpoints, such as the effectiveness and readiness of virtual reality and computational tools for training and rehabilitation versus practical control strategies for active prosthetics, indicating debates on technology readiness and translational gaps in clinical adoption.

Source Title: An Interdisciplinary Approach and Advanced Techniques for Enhanced 3D-Printed Upper Limb Prosthetic Socket Design: A Literature Review
Main Topic Area: Multiple (design methods, customization, accessibility, user involvement, interdisciplinary collaboration)
Key Gaps Identified: The paper identifies gaps in: interdisciplinary collaboration processes and evaluation methods; materials science for 3D-printed prosthetics, including durability and suitable printing materials; quality control and standardization for 3D-printed sockets; regulatory and reimbursement frameworks for additive-manufactured prostheses; empirical evidence on long-term functionality, durability and rates/reasons of prosthesis rejection/abandonment for 3D-printed ULPs.
Key Limitations Discussed: Limitations highlighted include material properties and durability shortcomings of printed sockets; need for laborious post-processing to achieve acceptable finish and comfort; absence of standardized processes leading to variable quality and functional performance; workforce skill and training gaps for CAD, AM and digital workflows.
Key Recommendations: Recommendations include developing and validating quality control and standardization methodologies for 3D-printed sockets; targeted interdisciplinary research on materials, durability and long-term outcomes including abandonment rates; fostering interdisciplinary collaboration through institutional innovation, shared language and evidence-based evaluation; training and workforce development in AM/CAD techniques (implied across discussion).
Contradictions Or Debates: The paper notes tensions/debates such as claims of 3D printing being low-cost versus material and post-processing costs that reduce affordability, and optimism about customization/accessibility versus practical limitations (materials, durability, standards) that temper expectations.

Source Title: The Current State of 3D-Printed Prostheses Clinical Outcomes - NIH
Key Gaps Identified: The review identifies several research gaps: small sample sizes and limited high-quality evidence limiting generalizability; lack of studies on certain prosthetic types, notably above-knee devices; and heterogeneity in outcome measures and assessment tools that impede cross-study comparisons.
Key Limitations Discussed: The paper highlights key limitations: frequent device durability issues (component breakage); predominance of small, low-quality studies lacking randomized controlled trials and rigorous designs; and heterogeneity in outcome measures reducing comparability and generalizability.
Key Recommendations: Recommendations include: conduct well-designed clinical trials with larger sample sizes and long-term follow-up, develop and adopt standardized outcome measures and evaluation protocols, investigate long-term durability and wider prosthetic types (e.g., above-knee devices), and address regulatory and material challenges to support clinical translation.
Contradictions Or Debates: The review notes conflicting performance findings: some studies report 3D-printed devices outperforming conventional devices in able-bodied or inexperienced users, while others report conventional hooks outperforming 3D-printed hands for experienced amputee users, indicating mixed evidence and user-dependent effectiveness. The overall interpretation is cautious due to limited study quality and heterogeneity.

Source Title: Review of Robotic Prostheses Manufactured with 3D Printing: Advances, Challenges, and Future Perspectives
Key Gaps Identified: Identifies gaps in: standardization and regulation for 3D-printed prostheses; material optimization and lack of durable, biocompatible materials for long-term use; limited functionality and control (precision, sensor interpretation, integration with biological systems such as BCIs); economic and infrastructural barriers limiting global access and affordability; need for methods for dynamic/custom adaptive fit over time and standard methods for measuring/manufacturing custom prostheses.
Key Limitations Discussed: Highlights limitations: material durability and mechanical weaknesses of common printing materials; limited control accuracy and lack of sensory feedback in prostheses (myoelectric signal interpretation); economic barriers including equipment and material costs and limited infrastructure for production and distribution; regulatory variability and lack of standardization affecting safety and certification (implied elsewhere).
Key Recommendations: Recommends: research into novel, biocompatible and durable materials and multi-material/4D printing techniques; development of global standards and regulatory frameworks for safety and quality testing; investment in infrastructure and policies to improve access and reduce costs, including public–private and international collaborations; further integration of AI, BCIs, AR/VR for control and rehabilitation research.
Contradictions Or Debates: Notes a tension: 3D printing is presented as both a democratizing, low-cost solution and as limited by infrastructure, regulatory barriers, and upfront equipment/material costs—creating a debate about real-world accessibility and scalability. No explicit conflicting study findings are reported; rather the paper highlights trade-offs and implementation challenges.

Source Title: Sculpting the future: a narrative review of 3D printing in plastic surgery and prosthetic devices
Key Gaps Identified: The paper identifies gaps in suitable biomaterials and their long-term biocompatibility; a lack of robust economic analyses comparing 3D printing to traditional methods; insufficient large-cohort or randomized evidence to validate efficacy and safety, with most data from small case series; and needs for optimization of design processes and assessment of long-term outcomes and cost-effectiveness.
Key Limitations Discussed: Limitations highlighted include limited high-quality comparative studies and randomized trials; material and manufacturing constraints (material selection, mechanical properties, bio-ink limitations); time and cost trade-offs for CAD-based/custom implants versus simpler guides; and regulatory, legal, and ethical challenges including lack of standardized frameworks.
Key Recommendations: Recommendations include research to refine materials and design processes and to study long-term outcomes and cost-effectiveness; regulatory reform and coordinated frameworks for safety and legal clarity; expanded training and interdisciplinary collaboration between surgeons, engineers, and manufacturers; and economic strategies such as collaborative funding and open-source approaches to improve affordability.
Contradictions Or Debates: The paper notes debates over cost-effectiveness and patient acceptance: while 3D printing can reduce long-term costs and improve planning, some patients still prefer traditional prosthetics for perceived durability, indicating conflicting perspectives on economic value and user preference.
